taiko.name: Prehistory
taiko.lede: Miura's cliffs record land pushed up by great earthquakes. On the plateau stood a large Yayoi village, and in sea caves people fished and practised divination.

kamakura.name: Ancient & Kamakura
kamakura.lede: Misaki, a short boat ride from Kamakura, was Minamoto no Yoritomo's favourite retreat. This peninsula was also home to the Miura clan and Wada Yoshimori, who supported the shogunate.

sengoku.name: Warring States
sengoku.lede: In 1516, after a three-year siege by Hojo Soun, the Miura clan fell at Arai Castle after some 450 years. The place name Aburatsubo comes from a legend of that day.

edo.name: Edo
edo.lede: At the mouth of Edo Bay, Misaki became the shogunate's sea checkpoint, with an office to inspect ships, a beacon to light the night sea, and camps to guard against foreign ships.

meiji.name: Meiji & Taisho
meiji.lede: With the opening of Japan came Western-style lighthouses and Japan's first marine biological station. Kitahara Hakushu wrote “Rain on Jogashima”, and the Great Kanto Earthquake reshaped the coast.

showa.name: Showa to today
showa.lede: Jogashima became a fortress island and was erased from maps and postcards. After the war Misaki became Japan's top tuna port. A bridge came in 1960, and the island became a sightseeing spot.

moroiso.name: Moroiso raised coast
moroiso.headline: Rows of shell holes in the cliff record great earthquakes
moroiso.story: Holes bored by rock-boring shellfish that live at the waterline line the cliff in several bands. Each band is thought to mark a time the land was lifted by an earthquake, and the site became a national natural monument in 1928. Seismologist Imamura Akitsune matched the upper bands to the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake and the 1703 Genroku earthquake, but later studies suggest the lower bands most likely formed 6,000–5,000 years ago.
moroiso.see: The bands of shell holes in the cliff

akasaka.name: Akasaka site
akasaka.headline: A large Yayoi village stood just south of Misakiguchi Station
akasaka.story: The remains of a settlement spread over a plateau about 50 m high, some 350 m south of Misakiguchi Station. More than 130 pit dwellings have been found, including one huge building of 15.0 m × 12.2 m. Bronze bracelets, iron fish hooks, glass beads, charred rice and turban and abalone shells suggest it was a base for fishing and sea trade. The core area became a national historic site in 2011.
akasaka.see: Finds are shown in the Akasaka Yayoi room at the Hasse Civic Center

bishamon.name: Bishamon cave
bishamon.headline: In a wave-cut cave, people fished and read the future
bishamon.story: About 40 sea caves carved by waves are known on the Miura Peninsula, around 30 of them in Miura City. Bishamon Cave (a prefectural historic site) and Ourayama Cave yielded many tools of bone, antler and shell, and bones used for divination. Many human bones were also found, showing the caves were finally used as graves.

kainan.name: Kainan Shrine
kainan.headline: A noble from the capital, washed ashore in a storm, became Miura's god
kainan.story: Legend says that in 864 Fujiwara no Sukemitsu, on his way to Kyushu, was swept to Miura by a storm and welcomed by the local chief. After his death people built a shrine to him, and in 982 a hall was built on the present site. The great ginkgo in the grounds (about 800 years old) is said to have been planted by Minamoto no Yoritomo. Every 15 January girls perform the Chakkirako dance here; it was inscribed by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2009 and is now one of the “Furyu-odori” dances.
kainan.see: The great ginkgo said to be planted by Yoritomo; the sacred bridge over the Mitarashi pond (finials given by Mukai Tadakatsu in 1640)

kentoji.name: Kentoji Temple (the Peach Palace)
kentoji.headline: Yoritomo had three villas in Misaki: peach, cherry and camellia
kentoji.story: Minamoto no Yoritomo is said to have built three villas in scenic Misaki: the Peach, Cherry and Camellia Palaces. This is the site of the Peach Palace. The temple is said to have been founded in the early Edo period by Mukai Masatsuna, Misaki's naval commissioner (sources give 1613 or 1628), and the graveyard holds the Mukai family's stones. The main Yakushi Buddha was the principal image of a temple that the monk Gyoki is said to have built on Jogashima in the Nara period. Kitahara Hakushu's poem stone was set up in 1941 and is said to be the only one whose unveiling he attended himself.
kentoji.see: Hakushu's poem stone; stone towers of the Mukai family

honzuiji.name: Honzuiji Temple (the Cherry Palace)
honzuiji.headline: Cherry-blossom parties that took in the trees across the water on Jogashima
honzuiji.story: This is said to be the site of Yoritomo's Cherry Palace. Many cherry trees were planted, and feasts were often held to view them together with the cherries on Jogashima across the water; the second and third shoguns, Yoriie and Sanetomo, also came. The temple moved here in 1719. A bell inscribed 1344 (a prefectural cultural property) and a gate built in 1821 remain.
honzuiji.see: The temple gate and the hilltop grounds

daichinji.name: Daichinji Temple (the Camellia Palace)
daichinji.headline: After Yoritomo's death, a woman became a nun and lived here for over 30 years
daichinji.story: This is said to be the site of Yoritomo's Camellia Palace, whose garden was once buried in camellia blossoms. The consort who lived here is said to have become a nun named Myogoni after Yoritomo died, and spent more than 30 years here. In the early Taisho era Kitahara Hakushu, who lived in a nearby Western-style house, often came here on walks.
daichinji.see: A quiet temple near the foot of Jogashima Bridge

konenji.name: Konenji Temple
konenji.headline: Wada Yoshimori honoured the dragon god who saved him at sea
konenji.story: This temple is said to have been founded by Wada Yoshimori in 1190. In 1180, after joining Yoritomo's uprising and losing, Yoshimori fled by sea from Kinugasa Castle. Believing a dragon god had saved him, he is said to have enshrined an eight-armed Benzaiten holding weapons. Eight dragons are painted on the ceiling of the main hall.
konenji.see: The dragons on the main hall ceiling

fukujuji.name: Fukujuji Temple and the grave of Miura Yoshimura
fukujuji.headline: Resting place of the clan head at the height of Miura power
fukujuji.story: This temple is said to have been built by Miura Yoshimura in 1200. Yoshimura allied with Hojo Yoshitoki, and in the Wada Battle of 1213 he switched from the side of his cousin Wada Yoshimori to the Hojo. The temple keeps a saddle, armour and short sword said to be his. His grave fell into the sea below the cliff in the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake, but local people rebuilt it.
fukujuji.see: Yoshimura's grave is in front of the Iwaura bus stop; the temple is a 3-minute walk south

shirahata.name: Shinmei Shirahata Shrine (home of Wada Yoshimori)
shirahata.headline: The name “Hasse” is said to come from Yoshimori's victory dance
shirahata.story: Wada, this village, was the home base of Wada Yoshimori, the first head of the Kamakura shogunate's samurai office. In 1213 he rose against the Hojo and died with his clan in Kamakura. The shrine is said to have been built by villagers 50 years later, in 1263, in his memory. The town name Hasse is also said to come from a dance Yoshimori performed at a feast with the villagers after returning victorious.
shirahata.see: Nearby: Wada Castle site and the Wada Yoshimori home monument (1921)

raifukuji.name: Raifukuji Temple
raifukuji.headline: After the clan fell, the temple moved from Kamakura to Yoshimori's home
raifukuji.story: Wada Yoshimori founded this temple at Nagoe in Kamakura. In 1217, after the clan was wiped out in the Wada Battle, it moved to Wada, the family's home; it came to its present site in 1670. A statue of Yoshimori in court dress is kept here. There are also graves of Choshu and Hikone samurai who guarded the sea from a nearby camp at the end of the Edo period.
raifukuji.see: About 15 minutes' walk from Miurakaigan Station

hikibashi.name: Hikibashi
hikibashi.headline: The bus stop is named after a bridge pulled up in the face of the enemy
hikibashi.story: Arai Castle had sea cliffs on three sides, and its only land entrance was this bridge about 3 km to the north. Pull the bridge up and there was no way in. Hojo Soun's army could not cross after the bridge was pulled, giving the Miura side time. The bridge's name survives as the place name.
hikibashi.see: The Hikibashi bus stop; 5 minutes' walk to the entrance of Koajiro Forest

arai.name: Arai Castle site
arai.headline: After a three-year siege, the Miura clan fell here
arai.story: A castle on a 26 m-high headland between Koajiro Bay and Aburatsubo Bay. Miura Yoshiatsu (Dosun) and his son Yoshioki held out for three years against Hojo Soun's great army, but the castle fell on 11 July 1516, ending some 450 years of the Miura clan. The main enclosure is now the grounds of the University of Tokyo's marine station. A 1992 excavation found a mass of human bones at the bottom of a 5.9 m-deep pit, reported as possibly a burial of those killed in the battle.
arai.see: Dry moats and earthworks around the station; the Arai Castle monument

aburatsubo.name: Aburatsubo Bay
aburatsubo.headline: “Aburatsubo” (oil pot) is said to come from the sea's colour the day the castle fell
aburatsubo.story: One theory says that on the day Arai Castle fell, the sea was stained with the blood of those who died fighting or threw themselves into the bay, looking as if oil had been spilled, and so it was called Aburatsubo. Another says the inlet's surface is as calm as spilled oil. Today it is a still inlet lined with yachts.
aburatsubo.see: The walking path looking down on the inlet

dosun.name: Grave of Miura Dosun
dosun.headline: “Victor and vanquished alike, once broken, are the same clay”
dosun.story: The grave of Miura Yoshiatsu (Dosun), father of the last Miura lord. According to the war chronicle Hojo Godaiki, Dosun left a poem saying that both those who strike and those struck are like clay cups, which once broken return to earth, and then took his own life. The same book says samurai who later visited the castle ruins got off their horses at the moat and bowed, calling Dosun and his son honourable warriors. Every year on the last Sunday of May the Dosun Festival (memorial service and kasagake horseback archery) is held.

misakijo.name: Misaki Castle site
misakijo.headline: The area around City Hall was a castle of the Hojo navy
misakijo.story: The castle stood on the height overlooking Misaki port, around today's Miura City Hall and the former Misaki Junior High School. Hojo Soun, who destroyed the Miura clan, rebuilt it as a defence against the Satomi clan of Awa across the sea; for a time the Satomi captured it. With its fine view near Jogashima, Hojo lords seem to have come here to rest; Hojo Ujiyasu visited in 1565. It was abandoned after Toyotomi Hideyoshi's Odawara campaign.
misakijo.see: Earthworks and a sign near the city gym parking lot

shirahige.name: Shirahige Shrine
shirahige.headline: The stone that rings when you tap it was an anchor weight
shirahige.story: Koajiro inlet has long been known as a harbour where ships waited for wind, and as Misaki's refuge port. The shrine is said to have begun in the Tenbun era when a glowing sacred object caught in a fisherman's night net was enshrined; it is a god of safe voyages and good catches. The “Kankan stone” to the left of the hall rings like metal when struck. It was an anchor weight, said to have been offered by a boatman from Settsu (around Osaka) after the god asked for it.

misakiko.name: Misaki Port (Edo-era sea checkpoint)
misakiko.headline: Ships bound for Edo were inspected at Misaki
misakiko.story: When Tokugawa Ieyasu entered the Kanto region, he based his navy at Misaki under naval commissioners such as Mukai Masatsuna. Once the country was at peace, Misaki became the place to inspect ships between Edo and the Kamigata region, and in 1624 Masatsuna's son Mukai Tadakatsu became Misaki magistrate. The port thrived as a harbour for ships waiting for wind and for collecting Sagami Bay fish to send to Edo.
misakiko.see: From the quay in front of Urari you can see how Jogashima shelters the port

awasaki.name: Awasaki (beacon and cannons)
awasaki.headline: Jogashima's lighthouse began as a beacon on the island's eastern tip
awasaki.story: In 1648 the Misaki magistrate set up a beacon on this cape, considered the start of Jogashima's lighthouse. Thirty years later, in 1678, the fire moved to the western tip of the island. As foreign ships increased at the end of the Edo period, Jogashima guarded the entrance to Edo Bay. In 1808 the Uraga magistrate built a battery on the island, and from 1810 the Aizu domain, ordered to defend the coast, set up a lookout and held cannon drills on this cape. The present Awasaki lighthouse dates from 1962.
awasaki.see: The lighthouse on the rocks beyond Jogashima Park, with the Boso Peninsula straight ahead

jinya.name: Coastal defence camp site
jinya.headline: The young Kido Takayoshi and Ito Hirobumi are said to have served here
jinya.story: As foreign ships came more often, a camp was set up at Kamimiyada in 1847 as the base for guarding the mouth of Edo Bay. It was run first by the Hikone domain, then by Choshu, Kumamoto and Sakura. Choshu was popular for starting local industry, and when it was replaced by Kumamoto, a petition asked it to stay. The later statesmen Kido Takayoshi and Ito Hirobumi are said to have served at this camp.

jogashima_todai.name: Jogashima Lighthouse
jogashima_todai.headline: Japan's fifth Western-style lighthouse
jogashima_todai.story: A Western-style lighthouse planned by the shogunate at foreign request, on the site of the Edo-period beacon. Designed by the French engineer Verny of the Yokosuka Ironworks, it was first lit on 8 September 1870, the fifth in Japan after Kannonzaki, Nojimazaki, Shinagawa and Kashinozaki. The original brick tower fell in the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake; today's white tower is the second, rebuilt afterwards.
jogashima_todai.see: The white tower on the cliff at the island's western tip

tsurugisaki.name: Tsurugisaki Lighthouse
tsurugisaki.headline: One of eight lighthouses the shogunate promised foreign powers
tsurugisaki.story: In 1866 the shogunate agreed in a treaty with the US, Britain, France and the Netherlands to build lighthouses at eight places, Tsurugisaki among them. Designed by the Briton Brunton, called the father of Japanese lighthouses, it was lit on 1 March 1871 as Japan's seventh Western-style lighthouse. The first stone tower fell in the Great Kanto Earthquake; the present octagonal tower was rebuilt in 1925. The line from here to Sunosaki on the Boso side marks the boundary between Tokyo Bay and the Pacific.
tsurugisaki.see: The white octagonal tower at the cape, facing the Boso Peninsula

rinkai.name: University of Tokyo Misaki Marine Biological Station
rinkai.headline: Japan's first marine biological station was born in Misaki
rinkai.story: In 1886 zoologist Mitsukuri Kakichi built a wooden laboratory on the site of the shogunate's ship office at Irifune in Misaki. It moved to Aburatsubo in 1897, and research continues today. More than 500 species of animals are said to live in the nearby sea. The grounds sit on the main enclosure of Arai Castle, where the Miura clan fell.
rinkai.see: The marine education exhibition room with specimens is open only on public open days

hakushu.name: Hakushu monument (Rain on Jogashima)
hakushu.headline: One song made Jogashima known across Japan
hakushu.story: In 1913 the poet Kitahara Hakushu lived at Mukogasaki in Misaki, across from Jogashima. That year he was asked to write “Rain on Jogashima” (Jogashima no Ame). It premiered on 30 October at the Yurakuza in Tokyo, and as the record sold, Jogashima became a dream island for young people. A monument was wanted while Hakushu was alive, but because the island was a fortress zone it was only built after the war, in 1949. Hakushu's own handwriting is carved on a sail-shaped stone.
hakushu.see: The Hakushu monument garden under Jogashima Bridge, and the Hakushu Memorial Hall

umanose.name: Umanose rock arch
umanose.headline: Before the Great Kanto Earthquake, small boats could pass through this hole
umanose.story: A spectacles-shaped rock gate carved by waves. Before 1923 small boats could pass under it. The Great Kanto Earthquake lifted the land, and now you can walk up to it. The same uplift exposed rocks in Jogashima's beach sand, and the bathing beach lost its crowds.
umanose.see: South side of the island, beyond Akabanezaki. Climbing on the rock is not allowed

hodai.name: Jogashima battery site (Jogashima Park)
hodai.headline: There was a time when Jogashima was erased from postcards
hodai.story: After the Great Kanto Earthquake, a battery was built on the island's eastern plateau as one of the forts guarding Tokyo Bay (begun 1924, completed 1927). Its guns were secondary guns from the battleship Aki, scrapped under disarmament treaties. People in Misaki were reportedly warned just for gazing at Jogashima, and the 1928 commemorative postcard of Misaki fishing port leaves the island out. The guns were removed after the war, and in 1958 the site became Kanagawa Prefectural Jogashima Park. The present observation deck stands where the battery's observation post was.
hodai.see: The park's observation deck: Boso, Izu Oshima and Mt. Fuji

ichiba.name: Misaki fish market (the tuna port)
ichiba.headline: For some years after the war, Misaki was Japan's top tuna port
ichiba.story: Misaki's town-run fish market opened in 1922. It became a major tuna base before the war, and from 1946 to around 1954 it was Japan's largest tuna port. Later, as ships grew larger and landed their catch at foreign ports on distant seas, Yaizu and Shimizu overtook it. In 1960 it was designated one of only 13 “Special Class 3” fishing ports in Japan. The present market moved here in 1994.
ichiba.see: The large building just west of Urari

ohashi.name: Jogashima Bridge
ohashi.headline: With the bridge, visitors to the island rose fivefold in a year
ohashi.story: Until then the only way to Jogashima was a ferry from Misaki. Work began in 1957 and the bridge opened in April 1960. It is 575 m long and 16–23.5 m above the sea, so large tuna boats can pass beneath. It was the first bridge in Japan to use steel box girders with steel decks. Visitors to the island grew from about 270,000 in 1956 to about 1.47 million in 1960, the year it opened. It has been toll-free since April 2020, and in 2023 it was recognised as civil engineering heritage by the Japan Society of Civil Engineers.
ohashi.see: From the bridge's footpath: the port, Mt. Fuji and Boso

marine.name: Former Aburatsubo Marine Park
marine.headline: The aquarium's Seven Lucky Gods moved to Kainan Shrine after 53 years
marine.story: An aquarium run by Keikyu, opened in April 1968. It was popular as a “circus aquarium” where fish performed tricks. As the building aged it closed on 30 September 2021, and its roughly 400 species and 4,000 animals went to other facilities. The “Animal Seven Lucky Gods” from inside were taken in by Kainan Shrine in Misaki.
marine.see: The building is closed. Arai Castle site and Dosun's grave are nearby
